what_its_for: Octreotide is used to treat several conditions. It helps control symptoms of certain tumors in the gut that cause severe diarrhea and flushing (called carcinoid tumors). It is also used for tumors that make too much of a hormone called VIP. In addition, it helps lower growth hormone levels in people who have a condition called acromegaly, which causes abnormal growth of hands, feet, and face.
how_to_take: Octreotide comes as an injection given under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a vein (intravenous). The long-acting form (LAR) is given as a shot into the muscle by your doctor or nurse, usually once a month. If you are taught to give yourself the regular short-acting injections at home, always rotate injection sites to avoid skin irritation. Common spots include the stomach, thighs, or upper arms. Wash your hands before each injection. Do not shake the medication vial. Let the medication warm to room temperature for 20 to 30 minutes before injecting to reduce discomfort.
dosing: Your dose depends on the condition being treated and how well your body responds to the medication. For most conditions, the short-acting form is given 2 to 3 times a day. The long-acting LAR form is usually given once every 4 weeks by a healthcare provider. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose of the short-acting injection, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not double up doses to make up for a missed one. If you miss your monthly long-acting LAR injection, call your doctor's office right away to reschedule as soon as possible.
storage: Store unopened vials or ampules of the short-acting form in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep them protected from light. Once opened, the short-acting form can be stored at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 14 days, but keep it away from light and heat. The long-acting LAR form must always be stored in the refrigerator and should only be prepared and given by a healthcare provider. Never freeze octreotide. Keep all forms out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid alcohol while taking octreotide, as it can worsen side effects. Be careful with driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or lightheaded. Talk to your doctor before taking any new medications, vitamins, or supplements, especially cyclosporine, insulin, diabetes medicines, heart medications, or bromocriptine, as octreotide can interact with them. Avoid eating large, fatty, or high-fat meals, as this can worsen digestive side effects like stomach cramps and diarrhea.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: signs of low blood sugar such as shakiness, sweating, confusion, or fast heartbeat; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst or frequent urination; severe stomach pain or pain in your upper right belly (which could be a sign of gallstones); slow or irregular heartbeat; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); unusual weight gain or swelling; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; or severe or worsening diarrhea. Also call if your injection site becomes very red, swollen, or painful.
when_it_works: The short-acting form of octreotide starts working within 30 minutes of the injection and its effects last about 12 hours. You may notice relief from symptoms like diarrhea and flushing within a few days of starting treatment. The long-acting monthly form takes about 2 to 3 months of regular injections to reach its full effect. During that time, your doctor may have you continue the short-acting form as well. Be patient and keep all your follow-up appointments so your doctor can check how well the medication is working for you.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially dizziness and low blood sugar, so regular monitoring is important. People with diabetes need to monitor their blood sugar closely because octreotide can cause blood sugar levels to go both too low and too high. If you have kidney or liver disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose. This medication is generally not recommended during pregnancy unless clearly needed, and it may pass into breast milk, so talk to your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Safety in children has not been fully established, so close monitoring by a doctor is essential in younger patients.
